question: Before the Brexit process, pilot training and qualifications were mostly standardised in the EU and the United Kingdom, and consequently licences were comparable in practice. Nevertheless, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and the UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) do not currently recognise each other’s licences, even though the training requirements are still very similar.

It is currently very burdensome to convert licences between the EASA and CAA systems. The process is similar to that of converting a third-country licence, and among other things it requires that the theory tests, medical examinations and additional training be repeated. This incurs substantial costs (in excess of EUR 20 000) and can delay professional progression by up to a year.

This question relates not only to individual professionals but also has a wider impact on Europe’s aviation sector. For example, Member States have traditionally benefited from the expertise of British pilots in relation to helicopter operations, including fighting wildfires and mountain rescue. At the same time, the sector is suffering from an ageing workforce and a shortage of new pilots.
On the basis of the above, I would like to request a response to the following questions: 1.

Is any action being taken or planned in the EU to promote the mutual recognition of pilot licences between the EASA and the United Kingdom, and how do you assess the impact of the current situation on the availability and safety of the workforce in Europe’s aviation sector?
Could the Commission promote a shorter and more cost-effective conversion process where the training requirements practically converge?
Has the Commission evaluated the option of negotiating a new agreement on the mutual recognition of pilot licences with the United Kingdom?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) 1. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement signed between the United Kingdom and the EU foresees some alleviations compared to normal trade rules with third counties. In the area of aviation, alleviations to standard rules concerning third country certification were only agreed for initial airworthiness, i.e.
the initial approval of new aircraft and other aviation products. 2.

Pilot licences issued by states that are not part of the EU aviation safety rules, can be validated under the conditions in Regulation (EU) 2020/7231, which ensures that their training is at same level as that of EU-trained pilots and which also allows for specific short-term validations in case of need to cover sudden pilot shortages in some specialist tasks. 3.

There are currently no changes foreseen to this agreement and the Commission is not aware of a particular shortage of pilots in the EU that would necessitate additional measures. The EU has a vibrant pilot training industry and has been able to cover any increase in pilot jobs.
